clinicalPearls: Characterised by abrupt, severe thrombocytopenia developing roughly five to twelve days after transfusion of a platelet-containing component
Most often affects multiparous women or previously transfused patients who have been alloimmunised to a platelet antigen
The great majority of cases involve antibodies to human platelet antigen 1a in an HPA-1a-negative recipient
Paradoxically the patient's own antigen-negative platelets are destroyed alongside the transfused antigen-positive platelets
Presents with purpura, mucosal bleeding and a profound drop in platelet count, with a risk of serious haemorrhage
First-line treatment is intravenous immunoglobulin, with corticosteroids and plasma exchange used in some cases
Further transfusion should ideally use antigen-negative components, and the condition is usually self-limiting over one to several weeks
reference.pathophysiology: Post-transfusion purpura is an alloimmune disorder occurring in a patient lacking a common platelet antigen, most often human platelet antigen 1a, who has been sensitised by earlier transfusion or pregnancy. Exposure to the antigen in a transfused component triggers an anamnestic rise in platelet alloantibody. These antibodies destroy the transfused antigen-positive platelets, but characteristically the recipient's own antigen-negative platelets are also consumed, producing profound thrombocytopenia. The destruction of autologous antigen-negative platelets is incompletely understood but may involve adsorption of soluble antigen or immune-complex mechanisms. The self-limiting course reflects eventual clearance of the antigenic stimulus and waning of the antibody response.
additionalDifferentials: Passive alloimmune thrombocytopenia from transfused antibody
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film confirming isolated severe thrombocytopenia
Platelet antibody testing, characteristically identifying anti-HPA-1a
Human platelet antigen typing of the recipient, typically HPA-1a negative
Coagulation screen to exclude disseminated intravascular coagulation
Review of transfusion history and timing relative to the platelet fall
Assessment for heparin exposure to exclude heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
redFlags: Profound thrombocytopenia with mucosal or gastrointestinal bleeding
Any suspicion of intracranial haemorrhage in a severely thrombocytopenic patient
Rapidly falling platelet count after recent transfusion in a multiparous woman
Bleeding failing to respond to standard platelet transfusion
reference.prognosis: The condition is typically self-limiting, with platelet counts recovering over one to several weeks, and intravenous immunoglobulin shortens the course, though the acute thrombocytopenic phase carries a genuine risk of severe and occasionally fatal haemorrhage.
pitfalls: Giving standard platelet transfusions, which are rapidly destroyed and may worsen the picture
Misdiagnosing it as simple immune thrombocytopenia and missing the transfusion link
Overlooking the diagnosis in a multiparous woman with recent transfusion
Failing to arrange antigen-negative components for any essential future transfusion
